notes.meaning: Jeremiah finished speaking every single word the Lord had given him for the people. He did not hold anything back or add his own opinions. Those who teach God's word must faithfully deliver what He says without altering the message.

The leaders of the people, led by Azariah and Johanan, called Jeremiah a liar and denied that God had forbidden them to go to Egypt. Their pride made them reject the truth because it opposed what they had already decided to do. When people have stubborn hearts, they often attack God's word rather than submit to it.

The leaders accused Jeremiah's scribe Baruch of turning the prophet against them so the Babylonians could kill them or take them away. Since they could find no real flaw in Jeremiah's proven record, they blamed his assistant instead. People who insist on sinning often invent wild conspiracies against those who speak the truth.

Johanan, the military officers, and all the people directly disobeyed the Lord's command to stay in the land of Judah. Just days earlier, they had promised under oath to follow whatever God directed, but they broke their word when they disliked His answer. They chose to trust human ideas of safety rather than God's promise of protection.

Johanan and his commanders gathered the entire remaining group of Judeans, including royal daughters and refugees who had returned home, and forced them to head toward Egypt. They also compelled Jeremiah and Baruch to go along against their will. The leaders may have taken the prophets as hostages, or to make it appear that God's messengers supported their journey.

The company entered Egypt in direct disobedience to the Lord and arrived at the border city of Tahpanhes. This journey reversed the Exodus, walking back into the land from which God had rescued their ancestors centuries before. Running away to another place cannot hide a person from God or remove the guilt of rebellion.

other.label: Catholic
other.view: An ancient church tradition recorded by early writers like Tertullian and Jerome states that Jeremiah was stoned to death by his rebellious countrymen at Tahpanhes for his continued warnings.

notes.meaning: The word of the Lord came to Jeremiah even after he had been carried off into Egypt. God's ability to speak is not limited to one country or holy place. The refugees discovered that running away could not put them beyond the reach of God's voice.

God told Jeremiah to bury large stones in the mortar near the entrance of Pharaoh's palace while the Judeans watched. This visible sign gave proof that Babylon's king would one day place his royal seat right over those stones. The contrast between solid stones and Egypt's crumbling brickwork showed that Babylon would overpower Pharaoh's fragile kingdom.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Many modern commentators connect this location with a large outdoor brick platform uncovered by archaeologists at Tell Defenneh, reading the Hebrew word as a paved terrace rather than an ordinary brick-kiln.

notes.meaning: Jeremiah announced that the Lord would bring King Nebuchadnezzar of Babylon, whom He called His servant, to set his throne and royal tent directly over those buried stones. Nebuchadnezzar is called God's servant because he would carry out God's sovereign purpose, even without realizing it. The exact detail was foretold so that when it happened, everyone would know God controls the future.

Nebuchadnezzar would attack Egypt and assign each captive to their appointed judgment, whether plague, captivity, or death in battle. The Judeans thought Egypt was an unshakeable fortress, but the very destruction they tried to escape would catch up with them there. Human hiding places offer no safety when God brings judgment.

God declared that Babylon would burn Egypt's temples and carry off its idols, showing how useless those false gods were. Nebuchadnezzar would take Egypt's wealth as easily as a shepherd wraps a cloak around himself, leaving the conquered land without anyone daring to stop him. Placing hope in false gods always ends in total ruin.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Several modern scholars and translations understand the shepherd metaphor to mean picking lice or vermin off a garment, picturing Nebuchadnezzar cleaning Egypt out completely.

notes.meaning: The invader would shatter the sacred pillars at Beth-shemesh, also known as the City of the Sun, and burn down all the Egyptian temples. These massive stone obelisks honored the sun god, yet they were helpless against the army God was sending. All earthly idols and pride will eventually fall before the Lord.
